For educators & curious dispatchers

Design a repeatable lesson.

Choose the route, schedule a disruption, and compare recovery strategies. One small text file keeps the setup, seed, and dispatch instructions together.

Keep this guide beside your experiment. Switch back to your existing lab tab to continue its run; “Open a new lab tab” starts a separate experiment at time zero.

One scenario format for every lesson. Start with a complete example, edit the route and interventions, then import the entire JSON text. The examples use 5-second stopping and starting delays. Control, safeguards and complete passenger comparisons explain how to evaluate outcomes.

01 / Quick start

From example to experiment

A scenario is a recipe for a fresh run. Every run starts with empty queues and evenly spaced buses in motion. Begin with one of the complete examples below.

  1. Copy a complete example. Use its Copy button, or download the JSON file and open it in a text editor. Copy everything from the first { to the final }.
  2. Return to your lab tab. In the Scenario library, choose Import scenario and paste the text. Change the name and description if you want your own lesson title.
  3. Choose Save as preset. This validates the text, saves a custom preset in this browser, and selects it in the library. Your current run continues unchanged.
  4. Close the panel, then choose Load scenario & reset. This starts the selected lesson at time zero. Use Run route or + 1 minute to reach the scheduled actions.

Saving and loading are separate steps. Export any run you want to keep before loading a new lesson. A saved preset remains in this browser, so keep a text copy for sharing and backup.

Complete lessons to copy or download

A baseline, then three timed actions

COMPLETE SCENARIO

Run a balanced route for 20 minutes, then introduce a hold, a slowdown, and a two-stop express instruction at minutes 20, 30, and 40. Automatic recovery is off.

For a clean baseline comparison, make a second copy with "interventions": []. Keep every other field the same.

Alternating express: a partial correction

COMPLETE SCENARIO

Hold Bus 1 for 60 seconds at minute 20, then check for recovery opportunities every 30 seconds from minute 25 through minute 60. This example has no timed slowdown or fixed-count express action. Stopping and starting each cost five seconds at served stops; protected drop-offs override skips. This lesson improves spacing only partially, and riders left waiting still pay a cost.

For a fair test of recovery, compare this file against a copy with "recovery_policy": null. Keep the same hold, setup, and seed in both.

Two gaps and passenger-preserving service

COMPLETE SCENARIOS

Each download matches a built-in lesson and stands on its own: 12 stops, four buses, fixed arrivals, 5-second stopping and starting delays, and a 60-second Bus 1 hold at minute 20. Open the downloaded text file, copy all its JSON, then import it as a preset. Keep the same setup and disruption when comparing the three responses.

  • Download two-gap-holds.json ↓: from minute 25 to minute 60, check every 15 seconds. Hold a bus for 30 seconds when its gap ahead is below 90% of ideal and its gap behind is above 110%. A 90-second per-bus budget and cooldown limit recovery; this is a partial correction lesson, not a complete cure.
  • Download drop-off-only.json ↓: from minute 25 through 60, check every five seconds for a gap above 3.3 stops ahead and below 2.7 behind. Give qualifying buses one drop-off-only location, with a 900-second safety cap. Recheck conditions before another correction.
  • Download announced-skip.json ↓: at minute 25, announce six lead-in stops for Bus 1, then serve every third stop for 12 locations, capped at 30 minutes from announcement. This lesson uses a timed instruction, with no automatic recovery policy. It demonstrates the cost of announcing too late: actual skips occur, but the default run does not recover.

These current-model service modes honor accepted drop-offs. They can still leave waiting passengers behind. Watch the pass-over counts, oldest queue wait and unfinished trips as well as completed-passenger averages.

Lesson choices

Show recovery, then show its limits.

Every current built-in lesson includes five seconds to slow into each served stop and five seconds to regain speed afterward. Start with the complete balanced recipe, edit it, or export any loaded lesson. A genuine bypass avoids both penalties; an accepted drop-off or manual stop hold makes the location served and pays both.

  • One delay → bunching: a minute-20 hold compounds. Compare with coordinated holds, which holds Buses 2–4 for 60 seconds at minute 25. This fixed script improves minutes 30–60 in the supplied setup; it is not an automatic dispatcher or permanent cure.
  • One-stop drop-off-only correction versus six-stop overcorrection: both can improve spacing, but the longer restriction increases passenger journey time in this lesson. A lower headway-variation percentage is not enough evidence.
  • Six-stop notice versus short announced skips: the latter announces one lead-in location followed by a two-location skip/serve pattern, rechecking both gaps before a later assignment. Both really bypass stops in the supplied run; only the shorter strategy recovers spacing effectively.
  • Bounded boarding limits new boarding starts while keeping accepted drop-offs. The event controller may cancel early when spacing recovers or eligible following service is inadequate.
  • Short-trip event holds and holds declined by safeguards show how onboard cost changes a decision. These two lessons use different ride and demand assumptions: compare each against its own uncontrolled copy, not directly against one another.

For a matched passenger comparison, retain the minute-20 Bus 1 hold and the exact setup/seed. In the copy, set recovery_policy to null and remove later recovery instructions (for coordinated holds, remove only the three minute-25 holds). Use the same cohort boundary of 1,200 seconds and inclusive arrival cutoff of 3,600 seconds, then drain both runs. Whole-journey means include the original queue wait. Do not compare completed-only means while riders remain unfinished. Random lessons reproduce seed 42; different seeds and settings can change the outcome.

More complete teaching examples

These variants use the same language and protected drop-offs: timed actions, alternating service, selective holds, drop-off-only, announced skips. They use zero stop/start penalties to isolate the service interventions; the main presets use five seconds each.

03 / File & route setup

Give the lesson a clear starting point

The format is JSON: keep the exact field names and double quotes, write numbers without quotes, and use no comments or trailing commas. Unknown fields are rejected so a misspelled setting cannot silently change your lesson.

Required sections and optional notes
Fields at the outermost level
Field What to write
format Exactly "Bus Bunching Lab scenario".
name A nonblank title, 1–100 characters.
description Lesson instructions, up to 4,000 characters. An empty string is allowed.
setup An object containing all ten route settings below.
model Physical assumptions; see the control reference.
observation Cohort boundary, arrival cutoff or null, and drain time bound.
interventions A list of timed actions. Use [] for none.
recovery_policy One recovery-rule object, or null to turn automatic recovery off.
notes (optional) Up to 4,000 characters of documentation. Notes do not control the model.

Every field above except notes is required. Empty intervention lists and a null recovery policy must still be written explicitly.

All ten setup fields, units, and allowed values
All settings are required inside setup
Field Meaning and range
stops Number of stops around the loop. Integer, 3–40.
buses Number of buses. Integer, 1–16.
travel_seconds_per_segment Travel time between adjacent stops, in seconds. 1–600.
passengers_per_stop_per_minute Arrival rate at each stop, in passengers per minute. 0–60; zero means no new passengers.
arrival_pattern "fixed" for regular intervals, synchronized across stops; "poisson" for independent random exponential intervals.
boarding_seconds_per_passenger Time to board one passenger, in seconds. 0–30.
debarking_seconds_per_passenger Time for one passenger to leave a bus, in seconds. 0–30.
ride_length_stops Fixed ride length, or the setting used to generate random rides. Integer, 1 through stops − 1.
ride_pattern "fixed" uses the chosen ride length. "random" picks a uniform integer from 1 through min(2 × ride_length_stops − 1, stops − 1).
random_seed Repeatable random sequence. Integer, 1–2,147,483,647.

Ranges include their endpoints. Numeric fields may have decimals unless marked “integer.” Changing the seed changes random arrivals and rides; it has no effect when both patterns are fixed.

Keep the experiment comparable. Start with identical setup and seed, then change one intervention or recovery rule. Bus capacity is unlimited, overtaking is allowed, and debarking happens before boarding, one passenger at a time.

04 / Timed interventions

Tell dispatch what to do, and when

Each entry in interventions needs at_seconds, bus, action, and the parameters for that action. Time is measured from the start of the run; bus numbers start at 1.

at_seconds can be any number from 0 through 604,800 (seven days). bus must be an integer from 1 through your configured bus count. Actions are sorted by time; those at the same time run in listed order, before automatic decisions at that time.

Hold: add time at a service stop

FRAGMENT · ONE INTERVENTION

{ "at_seconds": 1200, "bus": 1, "action": "hold", "seconds": 60 }

seconds must be greater than 0 and at most 3,600. If the bus is moving, the hold begins at its next service stop. If stopped, it begins now. Passengers continue boarding during a hold; the bus leaves only when both the hold and service are finished.

Repeated holds add to the remaining active or queued hold. Service time overlaps the hold, so a 60-second hold does not necessarily add 60 seconds to the final departure time.

Slow: multiply remaining segment travel

FRAGMENT · ONE INTERVENTION

{ "at_seconds": 1800, "bus": 2, "action": "slow", "multiplier": 2 }

multiplier is a number from 1 through 10. While moving, it multiplies the time still left on the current segment. If 10 seconds remain, a multiplier of 2 makes that 20 seconds. At a stop, it applies to the next segment instead.

Repeated slowdowns while moving multiply the remaining time again. While stopped, a new slowdown replaces the pending multiplier for the next segment. A multiplier of 1 does not undo an earlier slowdown already applied in motion.

Express: serve a stop, then skip a fixed count

FRAGMENT · ONE INTERVENTION

{ "at_seconds": 2400, "bus": 1, "action": "express", "stops": 2 }

stops is an integer from 1 through setup.stops − 1. A stopped bus serves its current stop, then skips that many consecutive stops. A moving bus serves its next service stop first, then begins skipping. It still travels every segment; a true bypass avoids service plus both maneuver penalties.

Accepted destinations remain served as exceptions to a skip pattern. Passengers whose destinations would be skipped cannot newly board. Every passenger already aboard keeps their destination.

A timed express action is a fixed count. It does not wait for the gap to recover, and it replaces any alternating recovery mode on that bus.

Drop-off-only service

FRAGMENT · ONE INTERVENTION

{
  "at_seconds": 1500, "bus": 1, "action": "drop_off_only",
  "stops": 3, "until_recovered": false, "max_seconds": 600
}

Honor every onboard destination but admit no new passengers. The count includes the current stop if stopped, or the next stop if moving. stops is an integer from 1 to 400; it counts stop locations passed, including locations with no drop-offs. A passenger already boarding finishes boarding and keeps that trip.

The following bus may gain passengers and slow down while this bus saves boarding time. This is useful for a bus with a large gap ahead and a close follower; it does not guarantee lower passenger time.

Announce a skip pattern in advance

FRAGMENT · ONE INTERVENTION

{
  "at_seconds": 1500, "bus": 1, "action": "announced_skip",
  "lead_stops": 6, "serve_every": 3, "for_stops": 12,
  "until_recovered": false, "max_seconds": 1800
}

The anchor is the current service stop, or the next stop if moving. Serve that anchor, then serve lead_stops upcoming locations normally. After the lead-in, skip serve_every − 1 locations, serve one, and repeat. serve_every: 2 alternates; 3 serves every third location. for_stops counts active locations after the lead-in, including skipped locations; it is an integer from 1 to 400.

With anchor stop 1 on a 12-stop loop and six lead-in stops, stops 2–7 have normal service. Then skip 8 and 9, serve 10, skip 11 and 12, serve 1, and repeat. The pattern follows successive encounters, including across the route wrap; with a route size not divisible by the pattern, a station's service can change each lap. lead_stops is an integer from 0 to setup.stops − 1; serve_every is an integer from 2 through setup.stops.

Boarding eligibility changes at announcement, including during the lead-in. A waiting passenger boards only if the first upcoming visit to their destination will be served under the plan. A later visit on another lap does not qualify. Accepted riders keep their promised drop-offs: a nominal skipped stop becomes a drop-off-only exception when a rider needs it. That exception does not allow boarding. Shortening or canceling a plan restores service; a new plan continues protecting every rider already accepted.

The bus still travels every route segment. Skipping saves service time, not distance, and a true bypass avoids both stopping and starting penalties. All these restrictions protect accepted drop-offs.

Duration, recovery and returning to normal

For either new service action, until_recovered: true ignores the stop count. It ends at an arrival when the forward gap is at most 110% of ideal. It is not “whichever comes first, count or recovery.” With false, use the fixed stop count, or null for ongoing service. Ongoing service lasts until canceled or its time cap expires. Every instruction requires max_seconds, a number from 1 through 604,800. This cap starts at announcement and includes lead-in, service and holds; it applies even if recovery never occurs. Reaching the cap restores normal service.

FRAGMENT · ONE INTERVENTION

{ "at_seconds": 3000, "bus": 1, "action": "normal_service" }

This cancels restrictive service, including express. It does not cancel an active or queued hold. There is no numeric parameter. Use it as an explicit ending for ongoing service or to stop a plan early.

Use at most 1,000 timed interventions, including manual dispatches recorded during the run. Combined queued holds or multiplied segment travel cannot exceed seven days. If a scheduled combination would exceed that limit, the action is skipped with an explanation in Dispatch history.

05 / Automatic recovery

Choose a spatial polling rule

Set recovery_policy to null for no automatic dispatch. Use the spatial rules below or the passenger-cost event controller. Each rule has one definition shared by all lessons. Editing description, notes, or optional rule_explanation text changes documentation only.

All recovery rules in this language
Rule Behavior
hold Polling comparison only: immediate circular neighbors, stable ID ties; leave the leader free. At most one action per visit, 30 seconds per action and 90 seconds per bus over the run, with two visits of cooldown. This spatial heuristic is separate from passenger-cost event control.
alternating-express Polling comparison: activate bounded alternating service above 125% of ideal forward gap; honor accepted drop-offs; stop acceleration when forward gap is at most 110% of ideal, or at expiry. Ordered immediate-neighbor gaps include the long convoy arc.
fixed-count-express Polling comparison: above 125% ideal forward gap, skip ceil(gap minus ideal) locations, honoring accepted drop-offs. A spatial heuristic without passenger-cost optimization.
two-gap Polling comparison: use one ordered snapshot, once per visit. Holding has leader protection, 30-second action limit, 90-second total budget and two-visit cooldown. Service restrictions preserve accepted drop-offs; no temporal coverage guarantee is claimed. Use passenger-cost for destination safeguards.
passenger-cost Event-based heuristic at stop arrivals and release opportunities. Use observed usable service and predicted eligible follower times, bounded onboard-cost versus queue-benefit holding, repeat budgets, destination-specific coverage and repeated-denial safeguards. Unknown or unsuitable coverage restores normal service. Predictions use current information, not future demand. This is illustrative and not an optimizer.

Ideal gap = stops ÷ buses. Forward gap is the distance to the immediate bus ahead, measured in stop units. Gap behind is distance to the immediate follower. With 12 stops and 4 buses, the ideal gap is 3 stops.

At each scheduled check, a bus is eligible only if it is at a service stop and has no active or queued hold or restrictive service. Buses travelling between stops are skipped for that check.

Test both gaps, then choose a response

FRAGMENT · REPLACE RECOVERY_POLICY

"recovery_policy": {
  "rule": "two-gap",
  "condition": {
    "ahead": "large", "behind": "small",
    "small_ratio": 0.9, "large_ratio": 1.1
  },
  "response": {
    "action": "drop_off_only", "stops": 1,
    "until_recovered": false, "max_seconds": 900
  },
  "start_seconds": 1500, "end_seconds": 3600,
  "check_every_seconds": 5
}

Each direction is "small", "large" or "any"; all selected conditions must match, and at least one direction must be tested. Small means strictly less than small_ratio × ideal; large means strictly greater than large_ratio × ideal. Equality does not trigger. On a 12-stop/four-bus route, ratios 0.9 and 1.1 mean below 2.7 stops and above 3.3 stops respectively. These are spatial distances, not elapsed time.

small_ratio must be greater than 0 and at most 1; large_ratio must be from 1 to 10, and larger than small_ratio. Choose a hold response with seconds, or drop_off_only / announced_skip with all their fields shown above. A response has no bus or at_seconds: it targets each qualifying bus at that check.

Candidates are evaluated from one common snapshot. The policy acts only at service stops, at most once per visit, and never overrides another hold or restrictive mode. Automatic restrictive service reserves at least one unrestricted local bus. With one bus, no two-gap intervention is activated. Manual instructions can still remove all boarding service, so watch queue waits. Ending the check schedule prevents new activations; instructions already issued continue to their own ending or cap.

Paste this into a complete recipe. For holds, small ahead plus large behind is a useful starting condition. For reducing boarding or skipping, try large ahead plus small behind. These are experiments, not guarantees of better passenger outcomes.

Schedule fields, check limits, and exact endpoints

FRAGMENT · REPLACE RECOVERY_POLICY

"recovery_policy": {
  "rule": "hold",
  "start_seconds": 1500,
  "end_seconds": 3600,
  "check_every_seconds": 30
}

start_seconds is from 0 through 604,800. end_seconds is from the start time through 604,800. check_every_seconds is from 1 through 604,800. These are seconds, and fractions are allowed.

A check happens at the start, then after each interval while the check time is at or before the end. The end is included only when an interval lands on it. Start 100, end 220, interval 40 gives checks at 100, 140, 180, and 220. End 225 gives the same checks, with no extra check at 225.

The file must satisfy (end_seconds − start_seconds) ÷ check_every_seconds ≤ 10,000, allowing at most 10,001 checks. Listed manual actions at a timestamp run before its automatic decision batch, after mandatory arrivals and door completions.

rule and all three schedule fields are required. The optional rule_explanation documents the rule; it cannot customize the formula. These are polling fields. The event controller uses start/end and an options object without check_every_seconds. Each recipe has one recovery policy.

06 / Control and comparisons

Control service. Count every passenger.

Built-in teaching lessons use stopping and starting delays of five seconds each. Every recipe uses deterministic immediate circular neighbors, protects accepted destinations and supports the same physical assumptions and controls. Keep route settings and passenger demand identical when comparing recovery strategies.

Start with a complete download, edit its text, then paste the whole file into Import scenario. These examples share a minute-20 disruption but deliberately vary their assumptions: the holding lesson uses fixed one-stop rides, the boarding/pattern lessons use fixed four-stop rides, and the physical lesson uses random demand. Each has an explicit minute-60 arrival cutoff. All values are illustrative, not calibrated observations or an optimized policy.

  • Bounded passenger-cost holding: short fixed rides, event decisions, 60-second action/visit caps, a 900-second per-bus budget and a finite cohort. This illustrates reduced onboard hold cost.
  • Limited boarding with destination safeguards: five new riders per visit, protected drop-offs.
  • Announced pattern with eligible following service: two lead-in locations, then alternating service for up to six locations. Recovery and coverage safeguards may end a plan before its first bypass.
  • Optional seats, stop overhead, and no overtaking: change one assumption at a time.
How gaps and the controller work

Every bus has one immediate neighbor ahead and behind. For four buses together on a 12-stop loop, the forward gaps are 0, 0, 0, and 12, rather than four zeros. With overtaking allowed, exact ties use bus ID order; the last tied ID owns the empty arc. Without overtaking, saved physical road order retains the real leader across the route boundary. A single bus has the full route gap in both directions.

In service plans, until_recovered ends when the forward gap is at most 110% of ideal spacing. The rear gap need not be normal: a tail bus may have caught up even while a large gap remains behind it. A convoy leader's long arc prevents a false recovery signal. Automatic holding leaves the front of every coincident group free of new automatic holds, including partial groups whose forward gap is still short. When an already held bus becomes that front, only automatic holding is released; its manual holds and door work still finish.

The passenger-cost rule evaluates stop arrivals and release opportunities, including zero-dwell visits. At one timestamp, passenger arrivals, bus arrivals and already-started door completions happen first, listed manual actions next, one automatic batch next, then new door movements and departures. The control window includes its start and excludes its end. At the end, only automatic holds and restrictions are released; manual instructions retain their own limits. Boarding or alighting underway always finishes.

Observed usable-service intervals are in seconds, and distinguish destinations. A full, drop-off-only or incompatible express bus is not usable service for that rider. Following-service estimates use current positions, known loads, seat releases, service, holds and announced plans. Future boarding and dwell are unknown. These are conditional estimates, not exact predictions; the controller consumes no demand random numbers and falls back to normal service when evidence or credible coverage is missing.

When overtaking is disabled, a reliable joint road-and-door forecast is unavailable. The temporal controller conservatively keeps normal service in that model. Manual interventions and physical no-overtaking still work. These comparisons measure the physical assumption, rather than automatic recovery.

Holding weighs estimated queue-wait savings against extra onboard delay and rear effects. Required service can absorb a requested hold. The lab separately records requested seconds and realized extra automatic dwell. Action and visit limits, a run-wide per-bus budget, and a cooldown prevent repeated unlimited delay. The ordered leader remains free of new automatic holds. This heuristic can lose to another strategy; compare passenger outcomes rather than assuming it is best.

Both predicted waiting benefit and onboard/rear-service costs use the additional hold beyond known required service. A fully absorbed request has no predicted spacing benefit, so it spends no budget or cooldown. A suppressed arrival can be reconsidered after passenger service finishes. Once a hold is accepted, later events reassess its remaining cost; only automatic time is released when the justification disappears. Manual holds and boarding underway remain intact.

Holding starts only below 95% of ideal forward spacing with a positive temporal deficit and credible follower. Service-saving responses require more than 110% of ideal ahead and less than 90% behind. Automatic restrictions restore normal service at 105% forward spacing, lost coverage, their span or expiry, or the control window end. Manual until-recovered instructions use the separate 110% threshold. All thresholds are illustrative.

Bounded boarding and passenger safeguards

A boarding_limit action specifies passengers (integer 0–500), stops (1–400 locations, or null for ongoing bounded service), until_recovered (true/false), and max_seconds (1–604,800 from announcement). It permits that many new boarding starts at each visit, including later arrivals. Boarding already underway is excluded from the new allowance and finishes. FIFO applies among eligible riders; destination-ineligible people retain their queue and original arrival clocks. All accepted drop-offs are honored.

An announced_skip uses the existing lead-in and every-Kth-location fields. New riders immediately follow the announced future service; existing riders can still alight at nominally skipped stops. A simple express command also protects accepted destinations.

Automatic restrictions require plausible following service for each affected stop and destination. Before actual pass-over, repeated-denial and queue/service-gap safeguards can safely restore normal boarding. Denials count once per person per actual bus visit and persist across new plans; capacity and policy denials are separate. One unrestricted bus somewhere on the loop is not sufficient coverage. Manual restrictions are not silently canceled. Overload, full buses or manual commands can make the bound impossible; the decision log reports breaches and their causes instead of discarding passengers or exceeding capacity.

Denial safeguard breaches count actual denied opportunities after a rider exceeds the denial or queue-age bound. A separate observed service-gap counter counts completed stop/destination service intervals longer than the configured limit, once per interval. Long gaps can occur even without an intervention. The longest observed gap also refers to completed intervals; an ongoing gap has not finished. Logged manual and capacity context describes the observation and does not by itself establish its cause.

Complete cohorts, cutoff and drain

The observation object declares cohort_start_seconds, arrival_cutoff_seconds, and drain_max_seconds. The cohort includes everybody present immediately before the common start, including riders aboard and completions exactly at that boundary, plus births through the cutoff. Choose the boundary before any treatment. Whole journeys retain the initial queue wait and original birth clock.

A cutoff is inclusive: arrivals exactly at that second occur; later scheduled births are canceled. New automatic control ends by the cutoff. Continue or use Run to cutoff & drain to finish the cohort, subject to the configured drain and run limits. Manual active instructions finish or expire normally. A null cutoff means continuous demand and no complete finite-cohort claim.

Observation exports include the clock horizon, cohort, created/completed/unfinished counts, accrued passenger-seconds, queue and onboard costs, decision context, and completeness. Full-cohort mean, p95 and maximum remain unavailable until everyone finishes after cutoff. A resource-limited drain is incomplete; completed-only averages do not replace full-cohort results. Match the full ordered birth records (ID, time, origin and destination), not just a seed, across policies.

Independent population integrals check accounting: arrivals equal completed plus queued plus onboard. Boarding counts aboard from its start and alighting remains aboard until completion, each person once. Accrued passenger time includes people still waiting or riding; spatial regularity is a secondary result.

Model assumptions and allowed values
Field Default / allowed values Meaning
stop_overhead_seconds 0; 0–120 seconds Once per served visit, even empty; before doors, overlapping holds. Fully skipped stops still traverse all road segments.
stopping_delay_seconds 5 in built-ins; 0–120 seconds Time lost entering a served stop, before overhead and door service. Zero for a bypass.
starting_delay_seconds 5 in built-ins; 0–120 seconds Time lost regaining speed after a served stop, added to the following road segment. Zero for a bypass.
bus_capacity null (unlimited), or integer 1–500 Seat reserved at boarding start, released after alighting finishes. Denied riders remain queued.
allow_overtaking true or false False constrains continuous road trajectories through slowdowns and the route seam; blocked buses restart when leaders move. Several buses can serve a stop together; this is not a single-berth model.
calibration_notes Text, at most 1,000 characters Record source/measurement procedure, or label inputs illustrative.
cohort_start_seconds 0; 0 through cutoff Common population boundary before treatment; at most 604,800 without cutoff.
arrival_cutoff_seconds null, or 0–604,800 Inclusive final demand timestamp; null retains continuous demand.
drain_max_seconds 86,400; 1–604,800 Maximum extra drain duration, still subject to the seven-day total run clock and population/visit limits.

Stopping and starting are lumped time penalties, not a continuous acceleration model. Stopping precedes overhead and doors and can overlap a hold. Starting extends the next linear travel segment after doors and holds finish. A nominal skip with a protected drop-off or manual stop hold is a served stop and pays both. Initial buses already traveling pay no starting penalty. Include both maneuver fields explicitly in your recipe. New exports include them explicitly. Built-in lesson values are five seconds each; these are lesson settings, not a new implicit import default. Compare one assumption at a time; seat limits, overhead and road queues can change which intervention helps.

Temporal controller option reference

These camel-case keys live inside recovery_policy.options. Durations are simulation seconds; counts below are integers. Omitted keys take the listed defaults.

Option Default Allowed values / purpose
response hold hold, boarding, dropoff or pattern.
decisionMode events events or polling; polling samples this same heuristic for cadence comparisons.
pollSeconds 30 1–3,600; polling only.
maxHold 30 0–3,600 per action; cannot exceed maxVisitHold.
maxVisitHold 45 0–3,600 requested seconds per visit.
repeatBudget 90 0–86,400 requested seconds per bus across the run; does not reset each stop.
cooldownStops 2 Integer 0–400 intervening completed visits between eligible holds.
benefitFactor 1.2 1–100 multiplier on estimated onboard and rear costs.
targetSeconds 0 0–86,400; zero uses observed service headway or an illustrative fluid fallback.
maxFollowerEta 300 1–86,400 maximum conditional following-service estimate.
maxDenials 2 Integer 0–100 repeated actual denials per passenger.
maxServiceGap 600 1–86,400 for eligible-service-gap and current queue-wait screening.
boardingPassengers 5 Integer 1–500 new riders per visit for automatic boarding control.
restrictionStops 3 Integer 1–400 stop locations.
leadStops 2 Integer 0 through route stops minus 1 before pattern activation.
serveEvery 2 Integer 2 through route stop count; serve each Kth pattern location.
restrictionMaxSeconds 600 1–604,800 from announcement until expiry.

Spatial polling rules are separate comparison heuristics. They use repaired spatial gaps, bounded holds and accepted-drop-off protection; they do not claim the destination-specific temporal safeguards of passenger-cost.

Spatial polling uses hold, alternating-express, fixed-count-express, or two-gap. The last uses the condition/response shape shown in the current-model two-gap fragment above. Automatic holds are capped at 30 seconds per action and 90 per bus, with two intervening stop visits; a coincident group leader remains free. Event-controller options are independently configurable and the short-trip lesson deliberately uses larger explicit budgets than the defaults in this table.

Event-control restrictions can restore normal service when the forward gap is at most 105% of ideal, or when coverage/denial safeguards fail. This is separate from a manual instruction's until_recovered flag. Ending a polling schedule stops new activations; a pending restriction finishes its own span/recovery/time cap. Ending an event-control window releases its automatic components. Continuing a lesson past its control window can allow bunching to return.

06 / Compare & share

Preserve the recipe. Measure the cost.

Use Export scenario to copy the active run’s setup, seed, recovery policy, all preset actions, and recorded manual interventions. It exports the active run, even if a different preset is selected in the library. While reviewing history, later retained interventions are included too.

The file recreates a run from time zero. It does not save the current clock, passengers, observations, chart settings, playback speed, or page layout. Use New window with this state to compare from the current point, and Export observations CSV to keep measured results.

Prompts for a class comparison

  • What happens to the bus behind the delayed bus? Follow both their gaps and their queue waits.
  • Does a lower headway variation also reduce total passenger time? Count passed-over passengers and people still waiting or riding.
  • What changes when you repeat with random arrivals? Keep the seed fixed for each pair of strategies, then try several seeds.
Passenger metrics and the cost of leaving people behind

Completed-trip system time is completion time minus original arrival time: it includes the initial queue, every later queue after any later queue, and all time aboard (travel, service and holds). The chart's individual observations and the mean include only finished trips. A faster average can hide riders who are still waiting or riding.

Oldest current queue wait is the longest current queue spell among passengers still waiting. Mean current queue wait averages those current queue spells across everyone waiting now. Both measure time since entry to the current queue. Boarding passengers count as onboard from boarding start.

Passed-over passengers counts one denial per passenger per restricted bus visit, including a bus passing without stopping. The same person denied by two buses contributes two pass-overs. The card's unique-people subtitle counts that person only once. A queue can grow after the bus leaves; those later arrivals are not attributed to that visit.

Passenger time accrued adds completed trip times to elapsed time since original arrival for every unfinished passenger. It includes waiting and riding, so people left behind remain visible. This is accumulated passenger time, not an average or a prediction of final trip time. Compare it at the same simulation clock with the same demand and seed. The card displays passenger-minutes (p-min); the observations CSV records passenger-seconds.

Compare completed trips, waiting and onboard populations, pass-overs and oldest queue wait together. The full passenger population is arrivals = completed + waiting + onboard. Lower headway variation alone does not establish a better result for passengers.

Completed-passenger averages exclude people who have not finished their trips. Headway variation measures spatial gaps around the loop; it is not itself a passenger waiting-time measure.

Sharing, backups, and import troubleshooting

Keep text backups. Imported presets are stored in this browser, with a limit of 100 custom presets. Browser storage may be unavailable or cleared. Sharing a custom lesson means sharing its complete JSON text or file; a built-in scenario link does not include custom edits.

If an import fails: read the message, keep the text, and check that you copied the entire file. Common causes are missing braces, trailing commas, a misspelled field, an out-of-range number, or an action targeting a bus that does not exist. A fragment from this guide is not a complete import.

File and run limits: scenario text is limited to 500,000 characters, with at most 1,000 interventions and a seven-day schedule. A run can also stop sooner at 250,000 passenger arrivals or 250,000 served stops across all buses. Export or review the results, then reset for another run.

After editing: import the complete revised text and save a new preset. Loading it resets the experiment. Changing fields in Route setup also takes effect only when you apply the setup and reset.
